meta.coverage: USD, EUR, GBP, JPY, AUD, NZD, CAD, CHF · 28 pairs (full G10 ex SEK/NOK) + DXY + JPYBASKET + GER40 + EU50 + XAU + XAG + XCU + USOIL
meta.regime: The energy leg did not just bounce, it changed character. Yemen's Houthis struck Ras Tanura, Saudi Arabia's largest refinery, the coalition hit Hodeidah port, and the IRGC claims two more tankers were mined in Hormuz: Brent settled 3.5% higher at 94.61 and trades 95.40, WTI 84.45. A risk premium about transit through Hormuz has become one about production and refining capacity, and that is a bigger number. The Canadian dollar keeps the top spot with a second leg, the Aussie short is dead - Q3 capex rose 12.2%, the most since 2011, and TradingEconomics has AUD/USD up 5.43% over four weeks, so yesterday's year-to-date-low premise was simply wrong. US markets are shut for Thanksgiving and liquidity is thin enough to exaggerate everything.

scenarios.then: December is sealed and January comes into play; EUR/JPY and GBP/JPY lower, USD/JPY still capped
The January leg comes out, USD/JPY pushes at 160 and intervention risk returns
Thin holiday books decide it; higher crude keeps capping any yen rally

meta.nextBigEvent: Tokyo core CPI Friday at 01:30, forecast 3.0% from 2.6% - the last data of the week and the test of a BoJ hike already above 85% priced.

dailyRead: Two things happened overnight and the first one changes the regime. Yemen's Houthis said they attacked Ras Tanura, Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery, and claimed strikes on the Riyadh financial district as well. The Saudi-led coalition said its air defences intercepted and destroyed four drones over Ras Tanura and did not confirm a hit on the refinery, but satellite imagery and bystander video show fire and smoke at the site and Reuters-linked reporting has a source with knowledge of the matter confirming an attack. That followed a coalition strike on Hodeidah port in Yemen and arrived alongside an IRGC claim that two more tankers struck naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz, which UKMTO has not confirmed. Brent settled 3.5% higher at 94.61 dollars and is now 95.40, up 0.83%, with WTI at 84.45, up 0.92%. Put that next to Monday, when WTI broke 80 dollars and Brent posted its lowest close since August 31: the energy collapse that every call on this board was built around has fully reversed in three sessions, and it has reversed for a different reason than the one that drove it. Until now the premium was about transit - friction, insurance, Hormuz traffic down about 40%. Attacks on Ras Tanura are about production and refining capacity, which is supply destruction rather than supply delay, and that is a bigger number. Brent is still 12.81% below a month ago but 52.53% above a year ago, so the level is low and the direction has turned. The second thing is that I was wrong about the Dow into New York. I published a bearish New York call and the index fell more than 1,100 points intraday to 48,883 before erasing all of it and closing 164.25 points higher at 50,183, up 0.33%, with energy leading sectors on the oil spike while the Nasdaq still lost 0.62%. The Worker scored it a miss of 915 points; the London call was right at minus 494. What that session showed is the rotation working in both directions - the AI complex is still being sold, but every dollar leaving it is finding a home in energy, health care and consumer names, and those are the Dow's weight. Now the third thing, which needs correcting properly. Yesterday I argued the only clean trade on the board was short the Australian dollar, on the grounds that October CPI beat on all three red-folder lines and the Aussie still made a fresh year-to-date low below 0.6600, proof the market would not pay for an RBA hike. That low was not a year-to-date low. TradingEconomics has AUD/USD up 5.43% over four weeks and up 1.68% over twelve months, and the Aussie is the strongest currency on this board over a month - it beat the Canadian dollar by 4.30%, the franc by 5.16% and the yen by 4.70%. Yesterday's fade was a pullback inside a rally, not a breakdown, and this morning the Australian Bureau of Statistics made the short worse: Q3 private capital expenditure rose 12.2% against a 4.4% forecast, the largest quarterly rise since 2011, with equipment and machinery up 23.1% and information media and telecommunications up 86.7% to a record on data-centre spending, while planned 2026-27 capex was revised up 11.8% to 223.7 billion Australian dollars. So the Aussie short is off: AUD/CAD and AUD/CHF both come out, AUD/USD is a range, and the Aussie is better expressed long against the kiwi, where the data gap is real. That capex print has a second use. What sold copper 18.68% in a month and silver 23.33% was the market deciding AI capital spending was about to stop. Australian information media and telecommunications investment rising 86.7% to a record is direct evidence of the opposite, and copper is up 0.99% with platinum up 3.38% this morning. The dollar is the odd one out. Core PCE went to a fresh 3.3% annual high on Wednesday with headline PCE at 3.8%, the three-month annualised core at 3.6%, Q3 GDP revised to 4.3% and claims at 189,000, and a December hike now prices at 94% to 98% on CME FedWatch with Polymarket at 94% and Kalshi at 92%. The dollar's reward for all of that was a dip to a one-week low overnight and DXY at 103.815, up 0.12%, while the 10-year fell to roughly 4.85% from 4.91%. When a currency cannot rally on its best data of the month, the December move is spent and only the 2027 dots are left. The Canadian dollar keeps the top spot and now has two legs rather than one: Macklem's Toronto remarks took December 9 from about 65% to roughly 80% on LSEG, and Brent at 95 dollars is a terms-of-trade tailwind for the only net energy exporter among the eight. USD/CAD is 1.42231 after a two-week high, and short EUR/CAD and long CAD/JPY are the cleanest two-sided energy expressions available - the oil exporter against the two biggest oil importers. Sterling and the euro sit in the same trap: a December rate market near 80% against economists who are not there, and neither currency being paid. The euro now has a dated risk few are discussing - S&P reviews France's A+ rating tomorrow, Fitch has moved its outlook to negative and Moody's holds Aa3 with a negative outlook. Yesterday Spain's IBEX fell 2.00% and Italy's FTSE MIB 1.81% against the DAX's 1.26%, with Banco Santander down 3.96%. That is why EU50 is short on its own evidence rather than as a copy of GER40: the periphery and the banks led the fall, which is the opposite of how a hawkish ECB is supposed to work. The yen got a genuinely hawkish line overnight - board member Tamura said rates must reach neutral soon, put neutral near 2%, pointed at CPI excluding temporary measures near 3.5% and said the Bank could assess each hike's effect within a few months - and USD/JPY slid to 159.00. It still will not break, because the Fed moves first on December 9 so the gap does not close, and because crude at 95 dollars is a direct hit to the largest oil importer of the eight. Tokyo core CPI tomorrow at 01:30, forecast 3.0% from 2.6%, is the last data of the week. The kiwi is the weakest currency here and the one place the oil move cuts the other way: the RBNZ's chief economist named oil price gains and a weaker New Zealand dollar as near-term inflation pressure, and Governor Breman has said the chance of a December 9 hike is high, so a 6% bounce in Brent since Monday is an argument for the hike the kiwi is still not being paid for. With US markets shut today and a half day tomorrow, the honest warning is liquidity: a handful of large orders can push a pair well away from where the fundamentals put it, so size down and do not chase.

today.headline: Q3 private capital expenditure rose 12.2% against a 4.4% forecast, the largest quarterly rise since 2011, and the Aussie was the best performer of the eight for a second time in three days.
today.read: This is the release that kills yesterday's short, and it kills it on the merits rather than on price. Equipment and machinery rose 23.1% and information media and telecommunications 86.7% to a record on data-centre spending, annual capex is up 18.6% and 2026-27 plans were revised up 11.8%. AUD/USD is 0.66439 and up 0.25%, AUD/NZD 1.21130 and up 0.39%, AUD/CHF up 0.29% and AUD/CAD up 0.26%. The December 8 hold has not changed and unemployment at 4.9% is still the hole, so express this against the kiwi rather than against the dollar or the Canadian dollar.

today.headline: The dollar dipped to a one-week low overnight despite core PCE hitting a fresh 3.3% annual high, with DXY at 103.815 and the 10-year down to roughly 4.85% from 4.91%.
today.read: A hawkish print that the currency cannot use is the most informative thing on the board. December is 94% to 98% priced on CME FedWatch and cannot go higher, the half-point bet is gone, and the three-month annualised core at 3.6% lands in the 2027 dots rather than in spot. Thin holiday books from today mean the dollar trades on positioning rather than data until December 9, and the Beige Book is already out. Long dollar only where the other side has a problem of its own - against the kiwi, not against the Aussie or the Canadian dollar.

today.headline: Board member Tamura said rates must reach neutral soon, put neutral near 2% and said each hike's effect can be assessed within a few months, and USD/JPY slid to 159.00.
today.read: That is a January argument, not a December one - December 18 is already above 85% priced, so the new information is the pace after it. The yen is quietly the second-best four-week performer here, up 0.77% against the dollar, and it gained against six of seven over the month. Two things still cap it: the Fed moves first on December 9 so the differential barely narrows, and Brent at 95.40 is a direct hit to the biggest oil importer of the eight. Tokyo core CPI tomorrow at 01:30, forecast 3.0% from 2.6%, is the last scheduled test.

today.headline: Spot barely moved after Wednesday's two-week high, but Brent settling 3.5% higher at 94.61 hands the Canadian dollar a second leg behind an 80% December.
today.read: USD/CAD is 1.42231 and up 0.05%, CAD/JPY 111.937 and flat, CAD/CHF up 0.10% - the move happened yesterday and today is consolidation. The fundamentals got better while the price stood still, which is the setup worth owning: Macklem's own oil caveat has been overtaken, and Canada is the only net energy exporter of the eight. The decision now rests on next week's Q3 GDP and November labour force survey, which Macklem named himself, so this is a trade with a dated invalidation rather than an open one.

today.headline: The kiwi did nothing of its own again and lost 0.39% to the Aussie, leaving it the worst four-week performer of the eight at minus 3.50% against the dollar.
today.read: There is no New Zealand release this week at all, so the kiwi trades as the residual of everyone else's news. The one thing that changed in its favour is indirect: the RBNZ's chief economist named oil price gains and a weaker currency as near-term inflation pressure, and Brent is up about 6% from Monday's low, which supports the December 9 hike Breman has already called likely. Being right on the hike has not paid for three weeks, so stay short against the Canadian dollar and the franc and let December 9 do its own work.

today.headline: EUR/USD slipped 0.13% to 1.09595 with December near fully priced, and the risk nobody is pricing is S&P's review of France's A+ rating tomorrow.
today.read: Both central banks hike in December and both are priced, so the differential is finished as a driver until the two dot plots. What is live is French fiscal risk: Fitch has moved to a negative outlook, Moody's holds Aa3 negative, and yesterday the periphery led the selloff with Spain down 2.00% and Italy 1.81% against Germany's 1.26%. Gas falling to 88.53 euros helps, Brent at 95.40 does not. The October accounts at 14:30 today are the only scheduled euro event, and 1.0900 is the floor that has held all week.

today.headline: Sterling held 1.30992 after a 19-month low of 1.3011 on November 23, with December pricing at 80% to 82% against 64 of 65 economists expecting a hold.
today.read: The standoff is the trade and it has not resolved. TradingEconomics is explicit that November was an 8-1 vote with Mann wanting fifty basis points, and the Bank expects inflation near 5% by the middle of next year, so the hawkish case is documented - but a currency making 19-month lows into an 80% rate market is telling you the market does not believe the follow-through. The Financial Stability Report at 12:30 today is not policy, though a calm report supports the December case. Trade sterling on the crosses against the Canadian dollar, not against the dollar.

today.headline: The franc was 0.12% weaker against the dollar and firmer against the euro, which is exactly the selective haven bid this regime produces.
today.read: Over four weeks the franc has gained 1.12% on the euro and 3.23% on the kiwi while losing 5.16% to the Aussie and 0.36% to the dollar, so the haven trade here is long franc against Europe and nothing else. The SNB holds at 0.00% on December 10 with core inflation at 0.5%, and crude at 95.40 widens the imported-energy gap without touching core, so there is nothing for the bank to respond to. Attacks on Saudi refining capacity are the kind of escalation that bids the franc; intervention, not rates, is the cap on it.

USD.when: December 9 at 21:00 with a new dot plot, and the quarter point is 94% to 98% priced
USD.note: TradingEconomics carries the Fed funds rate at 4.00% as the upper bound of the 3.75% to 4.00% range, held on October 28 with two policymakers voting for a 25 basis point hike. The October statement said activity is expanding at a strong pace, domestic spending is resilient and inflation remains elevated. Wednesday's data was hawkish on every line: core PCE 0.3% m/m in line but 3.3% y/y from 3.1% against a 3.2% consensus, headline PCE 3.8%, the three-month annualised core at 3.6%, the second estimate of Q3 GDP revised up to 4.3% against a 3.5% forecast, initial claims 189,000 from 202,000 and personal income 0.7% against 0.4%. The one soft line was spending at 0.3% with real spending flat. CME FedWatch now carries December between 94.4% and 98.1%, Polymarket 94% and Kalshi 92%, and El-Erian calls it a done deal. The tradeable consequence is that the dollar could not use it - DXY dipped to a one-week low overnight and the 10-year fell to roughly 4.85% from 4.91%. From here the dot plot does all the work, because November CPI only lands on December 10. Markets are shut today for Thanksgiving and close early tomorrow.

EUR.when: December 17 at 15:15, carried near 82% and described by Nordea as almost fully priced
EUR.note: TradingEconomics carries the deposit facility rate at 2.50%, with the main refinancing rate at 2.65% and the marginal lending rate at 2.90%, all held on October 29. Lagarde confirmed the Council discussed a hike and agreed unanimously to wait for the December data. Futures put December at about 82% on October 29 and Nordea now calls a hike almost fully priced, with a further move possible in March; all 71 economists in a November poll expect 2.75%. Euro-area inflation is 4.0%, a three-year high, with core at 2.6% and rising. The energy input the October statement leaned on has swung twice in a week: EU gas is 88.53 euros, down from 91.19 yesterday, but Brent is back to 95.40, so the net is still an inflation argument for the hike. The real euro problem remains the split - German composite PMI 55.0, the best since March 2022, against a French composite at 46.2. The October accounts land today at 14:30 and are the test of whether energy was the reason for December or just one of them. S&P reviews France's A+ rating tomorrow, French and Spanish flash CPI arrive Friday morning and Nagel speaks Friday at 14:40. Lagarde steps down on February 7, 2027.

GBP.when: December 17 at 14:00, where pricing is 80% to 82% against 64 of 65 economists at a hold
GBP.note: TradingEconomics carries Bank Rate at 4.00% after the November 5 quarter-point rise from 3.75%, and is explicit that the vote was 8-1 with Catherine Mann wanting fifty basis points to 4.25% - yesterday's file said nine-nil, and TradingEconomics wins. It was the first increase since August 2023. The Bank expects inflation to rise to around 5% by the middle of next year before falling back as energy effects fade, and noted activity data have generally been stronger than expected. CPI is 3.6% with core steady at 2.8%, unemployment improved to 4.6%, annual growth accelerated to 1.9% from 1.4% and wage growth slowed to 3.6% from 3.8%. December pricing is 80% on LSEG, near 80% on Bloomberg and 82% on one read, while a Reuters poll found 64 of 65 economists expecting a hold, February the consensus and 4.25% the peak. Mann has called for more hikes on inflation expectations; Dhingra points at disinflation. Sterling made a 19-month low of 1.3011 on November 23 and trades 1.30992, which is the whole problem - the rate market is hawkish and the currency is not being paid. The Financial Stability Report and FPC minutes land today at 12:30.

JPY.when: December 18 at 05:00 to 1.50%, above 85% priced, and January is now the live question
JPY.note: TradingEconomics carries the policy rate at 1.25% after the October 30 hold, an 8-1 vote with Hajime Takata dissenting for faster hikes, and its calendar forecasts 1.50% for December 18. A Reuters poll of 71 economists had 61 expecting that quarter point. The change overnight was board member Tamura, who said rates must reach neutral soon, repeated that he sees neutral near 2%, pointed at CPI excluding temporary measures running near 3.5% as an upside-risk signal and said the Bank could assess each hike's effect within a few months - which puts a January follow-up on the table rather than just December. USD/JPY slid to 159.00 on it. Wage growth at 4.6% is the fastest of the eight, core CPI is 2.2% and headline 2.3%, and services producer prices beat at 4.2% y/y on Wednesday. Two things still cap the yen: the Fed moves first on December 9 so the differential barely narrows, with the US 10-year near 4.85% against a Japanese 10-year around 2.71%; and Brent back at 95.40 is a direct terms-of-trade hit to the biggest oil importer here. Spot at 159.168 has not closed above 160.00 since September 1 and has not traded above 160.50 since the July 31 joint intervention. Tokyo core CPI tomorrow at 01:30 is forecast 3.0% from 2.6%.

AUD.when: December 8 at 05:30, where TradingEconomics carries 4.85% and only about 45% of a hike is priced
AUD.note: TradingEconomics carries the cash rate at 4.85% after the November 3 rise from 4.60%, an 18-year high and the fifth increase of 2026, and still forecasts 4.85% for December 8. The data has now beaten twice in two days. Wednesday's October CPI was above forecast on all three red-folder lines - headline 4.9% against 4.7% from 4.3%, monthly 0.5% against 0.4%, trimmed mean monthly 0.5% against 0.3% - with trimmed mean at 3.8% y/y. This morning Q3 private capital expenditure rose 12.2% against a 4.4% forecast, the largest quarterly rise since 2011, with equipment and machinery up 23.1%, information media and telecommunications up 86.7% to a record on data-centre spending, annual capex up 18.6% and 2026-27 plans revised up 11.8% to 223.7 billion dollars. ANZ and Westpac still expect a hold and one tracker prices about 45% of a hike, so the policy call has not moved - but the surprises are all one way, and that is the correction to yesterday's note, which read a one-session fade as a year-to-date low. The hole is the labour market: unemployment at a four-year high of 4.9% after employment fell 43,531, with three members having opposed the November rise. The November minutes majority of six of nine judged previous tightening was not clearly sufficient.

NZD.when: December 9 at 03:00 with a Monetary Policy Statement, where TradingEconomics forecasts 3.00%
NZD.note: TradingEconomics carries the Official Cash Rate at 2.75% after the October 28 hold, which surprised a market priced for a rise, and forecasts 3.00% for December 9. Governor Breman said the chance of a December hike is high and that every committee member agrees further increases are likely, with timing dependent on the outlook. The oil reversal is a genuine new argument for them: the chief economist named oil price gains and a weaker New Zealand dollar as near-term inflation pressure, and Brent has risen about 6% since Monday's three-month low. The November Survey of Expectations supports it too, with respondents at 3.05% by the end of the December quarter and 3.40% in a year, and one-year inflation expectations up to 2.92% from 2.60%. Against all that sits the weakest labour market of the eight: unemployment 5.7%, the highest since 2016, employment down 0.1% on the quarter and private wage growth 2.0%, the lowest here. Q3 CPI fell to 3.7% from 4.1% with core steady at 3.2%, though annual growth improved to 2.6% from 1.7%. The kiwi is the worst four-week performer on this board at minus 3.50% against the dollar and has no domestic release at all this week - a priced hike it is not being paid for, with nothing scheduled to change the argument before December 9.

CAD.when: December 9 at 16:45, now near 80% on LSEG against about 65% before Macklem spoke
CAD.note: TradingEconomics carries the overnight rate at 2.50% after the October 28 rise from 2.25%, the first increase in three years, and forecasts 2.75% for December 9. Macklem closed the gap to that forecast himself: speaking to the Economic Club of Canada in Toronto he conceded falling global oil prices could leave inflation below the Bank's last forecast, but reaffirmed the 2% target, admitted the Bank had sent mixed messages on core inflation and repeated that he expects firms to pass higher costs through in the coming months. Bay Street read it as hawkish, LSEG moved December 9 to roughly 80% from about 65%, and CIBC's Shenfeld sees a second consecutive hike. The oil concession has now been overtaken by events - Brent is 95.40 rather than the 88.67 of Tuesday morning, which removes the disinflation argument and adds a terms-of-trade tailwind for the only net energy exporter of the eight. The soft side is unchanged and real: core CPI 2.0%, trimmed 1.8%, median 2.0%, headline 3.1%, unemployment 6.7% and employment down in three of the last four months. Macklem named next week's Q3 GDP and November labour force survey as the deciders, so those two releases now carry the meeting. Current account tomorrow at 15:30 is the only item this week.

CHF.when: December 10 at 10:30, with TradingEconomics carrying 0.00% and no case for anything else
CHF.note: TradingEconomics carries the SNB policy rate at 0.00%, held on September 24 and unchanged since mid-2025, and forecasts 0.00% for December 10. At that meeting the bank said the current stance remains appropriate, noted inflation had risen on higher energy prices, forecast average inflation of 0.7% in 2026 and 0.8% in both 2027 and 2028 with GDP growth of 1.5% to 2% in 2026, and flagged high uncertainty from Middle East tensions, trade policy and exchange rates. It repeated that it remains willing to intervene in foreign exchange markets as necessary. October headline inflation is 1.5%, near a three-year high, but core is 0.5%, so the gap is imported energy rather than domestic pressure and the bank has nothing to respond to - and crude back at 95.40 widens exactly that imported gap without touching core. The franc's position this week is a haven bid, not policy, and it is selective: over four weeks the franc has gained 1.12% against the euro and 3.23% against the kiwi while losing 5.16% to the Aussie and 0.36% to the dollar. That is the honest shape of the trade - long franc against Europe, not against the commodity currencies. The cap is intervention, not rates, and there is no Swiss release left this week.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada Governor Macklem speaks
catalysts.note: The biggest FX event of the week. At the Economic Club of Canada he reaffirmed the 2% target, admitted past mixed messaging on core inflation and repeated that firms will pass costs through, while conceding oil could pull inflation below forecast. LSEG moved December 9 to about 80% from roughly 65%. The oil concession has since been overtaken by Brent at 95.40.

Above forecast on all three red-folder lines, with TradingEconomics putting trimmed mean at 3.8% y/y, a three-year high on the headline. Read together with this morning's capex beat it is the second one-way Australian surprise in three days.
Rose 4.2% y/y against a 3.6% forecast and 3.8% previous - the cleanest read on domestic rather than imported pressure, and the figure Tamura built on overnight.

catalysts.event: US October core PCE and prelim Q3 GDP
catalysts.note: At 15:30. Core PCE was 0.3% m/m in line but the annual rate rose to 3.3% from 3.1% against a 3.2% consensus, with headline PCE 3.8% and the three-month annualised core at 3.6%; the second estimate of Q3 GDP came in at 4.3% against 3.5%. Claims fell to 189,000 and personal income rose 0.7% while real spending was flat. December now prices 94% to 98%, and the dollar still dipped to a one-week low overnight.

catalysts.event: Houthi strikes on Ras Tanura and Riyadh
catalysts.note: Unscheduled and the biggest driver on the board. Yemen's Houthis claimed an attack on Saudi Arabia's largest refinery and on the Riyadh financial district; the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed four drones over Ras Tanura and did not confirm a hit, though imagery shows fire and smoke and Reuters-linked reporting has a source confirming an attack. It followed a coalition strike on Hodeidah port. Brent settled 3.5% higher at 94.61.

The index fell to 48,883 intraday and closed 164.25 points higher at 50,183, up 0.33%, with energy leading sectors on the oil spike while the Nasdaq lost 0.62%. The rotation out of AI is finding Dow weights rather than cash, and it scored yesterday's bearish New York call a miss.

catalysts.event: Australia Q3 capital expenditure and RBA Bulletin
catalysts.note: At 02:30. Private capex rose 12.2% against a 4.4% forecast, the largest quarterly rise since 2011, with equipment and machinery up 23.1%, information media and telecommunications up 86.7% to a record on data centres, annual capex up 18.6% and 2026-27 plans revised up 11.8% to 223.7 billion dollars. This is the release that takes every Aussie short off the board.

Said rates must reach neutral soon, repeated that he sees neutral near 2%, pointed at CPI excluding temporary measures near 3.5% as an upside-risk signal and said the Bank can assess each hike's effect within a few months. USD/JPY slid to 159.00. The first real argument for January rather than just December 18.
At 09:00, forecast minus 29.4 from minus 30.8. Secondary, but it sits against the best German composite PMI since March 2022 and the economy holding the euro-area aggregate up.
At 11:00, M3 forecast 3.5% unchanged and private loans 3.2% from 3.1%. Credit growth is the transmission check on four hikes, and it is still positive.
At 11:15. Normally noise, but it falls the day before S&P reviews France's A+ rating, so any fiscal language gets read through that lens.

catalysts.event: Bank of England Financial Stability Report and FPC minutes
catalysts.note: At 12:30. Not a policy statement, but the only scheduled UK event while an 80% rate market argues with 64 of 65 economists expecting a hold - and a calm report supports the December hike case.

At 14:30. The test of whether the Council's warning on elevated energy prices was the reason for December or just one of them. Lagarde said the hike was discussed and the hold was unanimous, so the accounts show how close it was - and with Brent back at 95.40 the energy argument is live again.
No US cash session today and a half day tomorrow, so there is no US30 call to make. Liquidity is thin enough that a handful of large orders can push a pair well away from fair value - size down.
At 01:30 Bucharest Friday, forecast 3.0% from 2.6%. The last data of the week and the only scheduled test of a BoJ hike already above 85% priced - and after Tamura, of whether January joins December.

France is A+ with a stable outlook at S&P and the review is dated November 27. Fitch has moved its outlook to negative and Moody's holds Aa3 negative, tied to a deficit-reducing 2027 budget. The euro's December is priced; this is not, and it is the live EU50 leg.

catalysts.event: French prelim CPI and GDP, Spanish flash CPI
catalysts.note: From 09:45. French prelim CPI forecast minus 0.2% m/m from 0.4%, prelim GDP minus 0.1% q/q, Spanish flash CPI 4.7% y/y from 4.9% at 10:00. The first read on whether euro-area inflation has peaked at 4.0%, landing the same morning as the S&P review.
At 10:55, forecast 5,000 from 4,000. Minor, but German labour is the one euro-area data series that has stayed firm.
At 14:40, after the French and Spanish prints. The most hawkish voice on the Council, so any pushback on a March follow-up to December matters more than the December move itself.
At 15:30, forecast 9.5 billion from 8.8 billion. The only Canadian item this week, and a wider surplus would support the terms-of-trade story Brent at 95.40 has started.

catalysts.event: US goods trade balance and a half-day close
catalysts.note: At 15:30, forecast minus 135.9 billion from minus 134.9 billion, with wholesale inventories alongside. US cash markets close early; treat Friday afternoon as untradeable.

catalysts.event: Canadian Q3 GDP and November labour force survey
catalysts.note: Macklem named both as the releases the Bank will weigh before December 9, so they now carry an 80% priced decision and every Canadian dollar position on this board. Employment has fallen in three of the last four months.

catalysts.event: Eight central bank decisions in eleven days
catalysts.note: RBA December 8 at 05:30 (hold expected), Fed December 9 at 21:00 with a dot plot, Bank of Canada December 9 at 16:45, RBNZ December 9 at 03:00 with a Monetary Policy Statement, SNB December 10 at 10:30, ECB December 17 at 15:15, Bank of England December 17 at 14:00 and the BoJ December 18 at 05:00. Six of the eight are priced for a hike, which is why the projections rather than the decisions are the trades.

geopolitics: Day 271 of a closed Strait of Hormuz, and this is the day the conflict stopped being a transit story. Yemen's Houthis said they attacked Ras Tanura in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province - the kingdom's largest refinery and one of the largest in the world - and claimed strikes on the Riyadh financial district as well. The Saudi-led coalition's account is narrower: spokesman Al-Malki said air defences intercepted and destroyed four drones over Ras Tanura and that fragments fell as a result, and the coalition has not confirmed the refinery was hit. Against that, satellite imagery and bystander video show fire and smoke at the site, and Reuters-linked reporting has a source with knowledge of the matter confirming an attack. The attacks followed a Saudi-led coalition strike on Hodeidah port in Yemen, which the Houthis named as the reason for hitting two Red Sea ports as well. Separately the IRGC Navy said two more oil tankers struck naval mines and caught fire in the strait on November 25; UKMTO has reported unidentified projectiles striking commercial ships in the same area with crews accounted for, but has not confirmed mines, and the same pattern of competing unverifiable accounts has now run for five weekends. The market read is unambiguous even where the facts are not: Brent settled 3.5% higher at 94.61 dollars and trades 95.40, WTI is 84.45 and up 0.92%, heating oil is up 0.24% and naphtha 2.14%. The reason this matters more than the previous spikes is the target. Hormuz is a chokepoint - Al Jazeera reported traffic down about 40%, with one analysis putting AIS-visible transits near 9% of the pre-crisis rate and Kpler measuring oil clearance at roughly half of pre-war levels - and a chokepoint delays barrels. Ras Tanura is processing and export capacity, and damage there destroys them. That is why a 6% move off Monday's three-month low has held rather than faded, even though crude is still 15.46% below a month ago. Diplomacy has not arrived: indirect US-Iran talks continue with Qatari and Pakistani mediation, mediators warned on November 21 of a risk of renewed conflict as negotiations stalled over Tehran's enriched uranium stockpile, and President Trump has said he is inclined to resume major strikes after the New Year if no agreement is reached. The FX transmission is now cleaner than it has been for weeks because the direction is consistent. Long the Canadian dollar: Canada is the only net energy exporter of the eight, Brent at 95.40 removes the disinflation caveat Macklem gave himself on Tuesday, and December 9 is near 80%. Short the yen's crosses with caution and long the oil-exporter crosses against it: Japan is the largest oil importer here and the hit runs straight through the trade balance, which is why CAD/JPY is the cleanest expression on the board. The euro area and Switzerland both import, but the franc is insulated where it counts - Swiss core inflation is 0.5% and the 1.5% headline is imported energy the SNB has already said it will not respond to - so the escalation bids the franc against the euro rather than against the commodity currencies. For equities it is a straight headwind: GER40 loses its falling-Brent tailwind, and EU50 carries that plus French fiscal risk into S&P's review tomorrow. For the metals it restores a floor that a 94% to 98% priced Fed had removed - gold closed 1.2% higher on Wednesday and platinum is up 3.38% this morning - and the honest caveat is that every leg of this reverses in one session if the mediators produce a breakthrough.

us30.headline: Core inflation hit a fresh high, Europe is closing lower and the global AI liquidation leaves the Dow on the back foot into New York.

london.note: Asian chip stocks were liquidated for a second day and the broad US market is down about 1%, so rallies are likely to be sold even though Europe opened higher.

check.note: The Dow has fallen steadily since the open and is near the day's lows, in line with the call; the 15:30 print decides what follows.

ny.note: The hawkish print is out of the way and the Dow went to its lows on it, so expect rallies to keep failing; thin pre-holiday books are the main risk to that.
